sec.title: Background
sec.p: Very old or frail patients with newly diagnosed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) frequently cannot tolerate full-dose R-CHOP, and long-term control with R-miniCHOP is suboptimal. We assessed a sequential, chemotherapy-limiting regimen using zanubrutinib, lenalidomide, and rituximab (ZR2) induction followed by response-adapted ZR2-miniCHOP.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This single-center, open-label, investigator-initiated phase 2 trial enrolled untreated patients aged ≥ 80 years, or 60–79 years with ECOG performance status ≥ 2. All patients received two 21-day cycles of chemotherapy-free ZR2 (zanubrutinib 160 mg twice daily continuously; lenalidomide 25 mg once daily on days 1–10; rituximab 375 mg/m2 on day 0), then four cycles of ZR2 plus reduced-dose miniCHOP. PET/CT after cycle 6 determined consolidation: two cycles of ZR2 maintenance for complete responders or two additional cycles of ZR2-miniCHOP for partial responders. Primary endpoints were overall response rate (ORR) and complete remission (CR) rate after six cycles; secondary endpoints included progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and safety.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Forty-eight patients were treated (median age 78 years; 45.8% ≥ 80; 70.8% high-risk by R-IPI). After ZR2 induction, ORR was 100% with 33.3% CR. By the end of treatment, ORR remained 100% and CR increased to 80.5%. At a median follow-up of 28.7 months, 2-year PFS and OS were 76.1% and 81.4%, respectively, with no CNS relapses observed. Grade 3–4 toxicities were mainly hematologic (neutropenia 29.2% during induction; 34.8% with miniCHOP), and no treatment-related deaths occurred.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Sequential ZR2 induction followed by response-adapted ZR2-miniCHOP achieved rapid, deep, and durable remissions with manageable toxicity in elderly or frail DLBCL, warrants further evaluation in randomized trials.

sec.title: Trial registration
sec.p: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2100047738), registered on 25 June 2021.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most prevalent and clinically heterogeneous subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma that predominantly affects older adults [1, 2], with more than half of the patients being newly the elderly. In clinical practice, the outcomes of elder patients remain inferior to those of younger cohorts, not only because of adverse disease biology but also because aging is accompanied by multimorbidity, progressive organ dysfunction, polypharmacy, and frailty, all of which limit tolerance to curative-intent chemotherapy. Although the current standard first-line regimen for DLBCL is R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone) [3], its toxicity frequently precludes full-dose delivery in elderly or vulnerable individuals. Thus, there is a significant proportion of very old patients being left untreated or given empirically attenuated therapy, which compromises cure rates. For fit patients aged > 80 years, R-miniCHOP is used as a treatment standard; however, long-term disease control remains unsatisfactory, with 2-year progression-free (PFS) and overall survival (OS) rates of only 47% and 59%, respectively, and clinically relevant hematologic toxicity still limiting treatment continuity [4].

Targeting Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) has been shown to be a promising strategy in B-cell malignancies, including DLBCL, given the role of B-cell receptor signaling in tumor survival and immune escape [5]. The Smart Start trial investigated a chemotherapy-free induction phase with rituximab, lenalidomide, and ibrutinib (RLI) followed by chemotherapy, demonstrating rapid cytoreduction and high response rates [6]. However, in elderly patients, ibrutinib-based approaches are often constrained by off-target effects, drug–drug interactions, and cardiovascular toxicity, particularly atrial fibrillation and hypertension, which can be prohibitive in frail patients.

In randomized studies for chronic lymphocytic leukemia and Waldenström macroglobulinemia, zanubrutinib has been shown to achieve superior disease control with lower rates of atrial fibrillation (approximately 2–3% versus 10–15% with ibrutinib) and fewer hypertension events, supporting its suitability for older populations with pre-existing cardiovascular risk [7, 8]. These advantages support zanubrutinib as a more appropriate BTK backbone for frontline strategies intended for elderly or frail DLBCL.

Lenalidomide and rituximab have complementary activity with BTK inhibition through immune modulation and enhancement of antibody-dependent cytotoxicity, providing a non-overlapping, chemotherapy-sparing platform. Consistent with this concept, the zanubrutinib-lenalidomide-rituximab (ZR2) regimen has shown encouraging activity in DLBCL, achieving an overall response rate of 77% in untreated patients and 50% in relapsed/refractory disease with manageable toxicity [9]. In our previous study, we reported that BTK inhibitor-based first-line therapy is feasible in elderly or frail patients, yielding 1-year PFS and OS rates of 81% and 88.5%, respectively [10]. Although zanubrutinib combined with standard chemotherapy (ZR-CHOP) has also produced favorable outcomes in newly diagnosed high-risk subtypes [11], these trials largely enrolled younger and fitter patients (median age 59), leaving uncertainty about safety and deliverability in the truly elderly or frail population.

An important clinical gap in this field is whether a sequential, chemotherapy-limiting strategy can preserve curative efficacy while improving tolerability and treatment completion in older or vulnerable patients [12]. In addition, giving ZR2 first may shrink the lymphoma and improve patients’ overall condition, so that the later reduced-dose miniCHOP can be started more safely and completed as planned [5]. Mechanistically, BTK blockade has been shown to suppress chronic active B-cell receptor signaling, lenalidomide increased T-cell and NK-cell–mediated antitumor responses, and rituximab provided immediate CD20-targeted clearance, together offering a coherent rationale for front-loading disease control and minimizing cytotoxic exposure in a population with limited physiologic reserve [6].

Accordingly, we designed an investigator-initiated, single-arm phase 2 study in which elderly or frail patients with newly diagnosed DLBCL received two cycles of chemotherapy-free ZR2 induction followed by response-adapted ZR2-miniCHOP. The primary aim was to evaluate the antitumor activity of this sequential, chemotherapy-limiting approach, using overall response rate (ORR) and complete remission (CR) rate after six cycles as key efficacy endpoints. Secondary aims were to estimate PFS and OS and to define the safety and tolerability profile in this high-risk population. We hypothesized that early disease control with zanubrutinib-based immunotherapy would facilitate delivery of reduced-intensity chemotherapy, resulting in deep and durable remissions with acceptable toxicity in elderly or frail patients.

sec.title: Study design and patients
sec.p: This was a single-center, open-label, investigator-initiated phase 2 trial (ChiCTR2100047738) conducted at The First Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice. The protocol was approved by the institutional review board, and all participants provided written informed consent before enrollment.

Between June 2021 and September 2023, patients were screened for eligibility. Following screening, those who were 60 years or older, had DLBCL confirmed by pathology and had not received any previous treatment, and were considered suitable for a strategy that reduced standard chemotherapy intensity, were considered eligible for enrollment. The main exclusion criteria comprised prior systemic therapy for lymphoma; primary mediastinal or primary CNS lymphoma, or active CNS involvement at diagnosis; uncontrolled infection; severe or unstable cardiovascular, hepatic, renal, or pulmonary disease that precluded study therapy; active hepatitis B/C with uncontrolled viral replication or HIV infection; known hypersensitivity to study drugs; pregnancy or lactation; and inability to take oral medication or comply with study assessments.

To define which patients were “elderly or frail/unfit”, we followed a simple, protocol-based rule reflecting expected tolerance to treatment in daily practice. Patients aged 60–80 years were eligible if their physical condition was reduced (ECOG performance status ≥ 2). Patients aged 80 years or older were eligible regardless of ECOG score (0–4). Beyond this age/ECOG rule, the treating investigators also used standard clinical judgment, based on other illnesses, organ function and overall physical reserve, to confirm that full-dose R-CHOP would likely not be well tolerated.

sec.title: Treatment and response-adapted strategy
sec.p: The regimen consisted of an initial chemotherapy-free induction followed by reduced-dose chemo-immunotherapy. Patients first received two 21-day cycles (cycles 1–2) of ZR2 induction: zanubrutinib 160 mg orally twice daily continuously, lenalidomide 25 mg orally once daily on days 1–10, and rituximab 375 mg/m2 intravenously on day 0 of each cycle.

From cycle 3 onward, patients proceeded to ZR2 combined with miniCHOP for four additional 21-day cycles (cycles 3–6). miniCHOP was delivered at reduced intensity and included cyclophosphamide 400 mg/m2, doxorubicin 25 mg/m2, and vincristine 1 mg on day 1, plus prednisone 40 mg/m2 on days 1–5, administered together with continued zanubrutinib, lenalidomide, and rituximab as above. The sequential design was chosen for early cytoreduction and clinical stabilization using a chemotherapy-sparing backbone, with the aim of improving tolerability of subsequent reduced-dose chemotherapy in patients with limited physiologic reserve.

Response-adaptation was based on PET/CT after six cycles. After completion of cycle 6, patients in CR transitioned to two additional maintenance cycles of ZR2 without chemotherapy (cycles 7–8). Patients in partial remission received two further cycles of ZR2-miniCHOP (cycles 7–8) to consolidate response. A short steroid prephase (prednisone or dexamethasone) before cycle 1 was permitted for symptom control at the investigators’ discretion. Dose-modification rules and supportive measures (including prophylaxis for tumor lysis syndrome, thrombosis, infection) were performed according to the predefined protocol. Routine primary prophylaxis with G-CSF was not administered to align with local medical insurance reimbursement policies; instead, therapeutic short-acting G-CSF and secondary prophylaxis with long-acting G-CSF were employed for patients who developed severe or febrile neutropenia.

sec.title: Response and safety assessments
sec.p: Disease evaluation was performed at baseline, after cycle 2, after cycle 6, at the end of treatment, and during follow-up (every 3 months in year 1 and every 6 months in year 2). PET/CT was obtained after cycles 3 or 4 and at cycle 6, and responses were graded according to Lugano 2014 criteria [13]. CT was used for interim assessments at other time points when PET/CT was not scheduled. PET/CT images were independently reviewed by experienced nuclear medicine physicians; discrepant interpretations were resolved by consensus review to reach a final adjudicated response status.

Cell-of-origin was classified based on immunohistochemistry using the Hans algorithm [14]. Genomic profiling was conducted by next-generation sequencing (NGS) at a centralized clinical laboratory (Nanjing Geneseeq Technology Inc., Nanjing, China) [15]. Adverse events (AEs) were graded using the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE), version 5.0.

sec.title: Endpoints
sec.p: The primary endpoints were ORR and CR rate assessed by PET/CT after six cycles of therapy. The key secondary endpoints included PFS and OS, defined from first treatment to relapse/death and to death from any cause, respectively. Additional secondary endpoints were treatment completion rate (proportion finishing protocol-specified therapy through at least cycle 6 and, when applicable, cycles 7–8) and delivered dose intensity of miniCHOP and ZR2 components. Prespecified exploratory endpoints included molecular correlates of response and survival based on NGS profiles, and cumulative incidence of CNS relapse during follow-up, given the high baseline CNS-IPI risk in this population.

sec.title: Sample size estimation
sec.p: This phase 2 study was designed to provide an initial assessment of efficacy and tolerability in an elderly/frail setting. A target sample size of approximately 45–50 patients (planned n = 48) was considered sufficient to estimate ORR with reasonable precision and to detect a clinically meaningful improvement over historical outcomes with R-miniCHOP, while remaining feasible for a single-center study. The trial was exploratory and not powered for formal comparative hypothesis testing.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Descriptive statistics summarized baseline characteristics and safety outcomes; continuous variables are reported as medians with ranges, and categorical variables as counts and percentages. ORR and CR rates were estimated with exact two-sided 95% confidence intervals using the Clopper-Pearson method. Time-to-event endpoints (PFS and OS) were analyzed using Kaplan–Meier methods, with 95% confidence intervals derived from Greenwood’s formula, and hazard ratios were explored using Cox proportional hazards models. Given the advanced age and competing non-lymphoma mortality risk, cumulative incidence functions were used to describe relapse and non-relapse mortality, treating death without prior relapse as a competing event; where appropriate, Fine-Gray models were applied for exploratory competing-risk comparisons. Prespecified subgroup analyses were exploratory and included stratification by age group (60–79 vs ≥ 80 years), ECOG status, R-IPI/CNS-IPI risk, cell-of-origin, and major genomic/LymphGen categories. For exploratory molecular analyses involving multiple comparisons, false-discovery rate control was applied using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. All analyses were performed in R (version 4.1.2).

sec.title: Patient disposition and treatment delivery
sec.p: Between June 2021 and August 2023, a total of 215 patients were assessed for eligibility. Of these, 48 patients were enrolled and received the ZR2-miniCHOP induction regimen (Supplementary Figure S1). All enrolled patients received at least two cycles of ZR2 induction and were evaluable for early response. Two patients discontinued study treatment after three cycles because of financial constraints and transitioned to standard chemotherapy. Three patients died from causes unrelated to lymphoma or study therapy (two from COVID-19 infection and one from intracranial hemorrhage), and these events were considered non-treatment-related. Three patients experienced progressive disease during protocol therapy, two achieved partial responses to subsequent alternative regimens, whereas one remained refractory and died shortly thereafter. Among patients who completed planned treatment and entered surveillance, seven later relapsed at varying time points (Supplementary Figure S2). For safety analyses, AEs during ZR2 induction were assessed in all 48 patients, and events during ZR2-miniCHOP were evaluated in the 23 patients who proceeded to combination therapy.

sec.title: Baseline characteristics
sec.p:
The median age was 78 years (range, 65–90), and nearly half of the patients (45.8%) were ≥ 80 years. Advanced disease was common: 81.3% had Ann Arbor stage III–IV disease, 66.7% had ≥ 2 extranodal sites, and 64.6% had elevated LDH. Prognostic indices further underscored baseline risk, with 70.8% classified as high risk by R-IPI [16] (3–5) and 54.2% carrying high CNS-IPI [17] scores (4–6). Functional vulnerability was frequent, as 31.3% had ECOG performance status ≥ 2. Among assessable cases, 41.7% were MYC/BCL2 double expressors and 77.1% were non-GCB by Hans classification [18]. sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p:
After two cycles of ZR2 induction, all patients responded (ORR 100%), including 16 patients (33.3%) who achieved CR and 32 (66.7%) who achieved PR. By cycle 6, 44 patients were evaluable; the ORR remained high at 93.2%, with a marked deepening of responses, and 32 patients (72.7%) in CR and 9 (20.5%) in PR, while 3 patients had progressive disease. At the end of treatment, 41 patients were evaluable, and all maintained an objective response (ORR 100%); the CR rate further increased to 80.5% (33/41), with the remaining patients in PR (Fig. 1A). No stable disease was observed at any assessment, and the progressive rise in CR rate from induction through end-of-treatment indicates substantial PR-to-CR conversion during the sequential, response-adapted phase. Individual response trajectories and treatment duration are shown in the Sankey diagram and swimmer plot (Fig. 1A; Supplementary Figure S3). Subgroup analysis based on the cell-of-origin (Han’s algorithm) was performed for the 41 evaluable patients. Among the 32 patients with the non-GCB subtype, the CR rate was 78.1% (25/32). In the 8 patients with the GCB subtype, the CR rate was 87.5% (7/8). There was no statistically significant difference in CR rates between the non-GCB and GCB subgroups (P > 0.99), indicating robust efficacy across different biological subtypes.Fig. 1

sec.title: Secondary endpoints and follow-up outcomes
sec.p: At a median follow-up of 28.7 months, the estimated 2-year PFS was 76.1% (95% CI, 64.7–89.5) and the 2-year OS was 81.4% (95% CI, 70.5–94.0) (Fig. 1B-C). Notably, despite more than half of this cohort having high CNS-IPI risk at baseline, no CNS relapses were observed during follow-up.

sec.title: Molecular profiling and response based on the LymphGen subtype
sec.p:
Baseline sequencing data were available for 41 patients (36 tissue and 5 plasma samples), reflecting the constraints of routine clinical sequencing in elderly patients with DLBCL (Fig. 2A). According to the LymphGen classification, genetic subtypes were assigned in these 41 patients, while 7 patients (14.6%) were categorized as unknown due to insufficient genomic information. In the overall cohort, the most frequent subtype was MCD (10/48, 20.8%), followed by BN2 (6/48, 12.5%) and ST2 (4/48, 8.3%). The TP53 subtype was identified in 2 patients (4.2%), and 12 patients (25.0%) were classified as unclassified (Fig. 2B).Fig. 2

Among 41 patients, 36 samples were obtained from tissue, while 5 were analyzed from plasma due to insufficient tissue availability. Specimens were unavailable for the remaining 7 patients. B Distribution of LymphGen subtypes represented in a pie chart

Given prior evidence linking MCD and BN2 to BTK inhibitor sensitivity, these subtypes were analyzed separately. At the end of treatment, complete response rates were numerically higher in MCD (80.0%) than in BN2 (66.7%) and other subtypes grouped as “others” (68.0%). Overall response rates were 100% in both MCD and BN2 and 84.0% in other subtypes, with no statistically significant differences observed.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Overall, the sequential regimen was generally well-tolerated, and no treatment-related deaths occurred. Grade 3–4 toxicities were predominantly hematologic and were more frequent after chemotherapy was introduced. During ZR2 induction, neutropenia occurred in 45.8% of patients, with grade 3–4 events in 29.2%. After escalation to ZR2-miniCHOP, these rates rose modestly to 56.5% and 34.8%, respectively.

Thrombocytopenia increased from 20.8% (grade 3–4: 8.3%) during ZR2 alone to 34.8% (grade 3–4: 8.7%) during combination therapy. Febrile neutropenia was observed in 10.4% during induction and 8.7% during ZR2-miniCHOP. Non-hematologic events, such as rash, nausea, and constipation, were mostly grade 1–2, and only one invasive fungal infection was recorded. Importantly, cardiac toxicity was minimal: a single case of new-onset atrial fibrillation occurred during ZR2, was controlled with rivaroxaban, and did not require treatment interruption, supporting the suitability of zanubrutinib in this elderly/high-comorbidity setting. sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This phase 2 trial demonstrates that a sequential, chemotherapy-limiting strategy with ZR2 induction followed by response-adapted ZR2-miniCHOP can deliver durable remissions in an elderly or frail population with newly diagnosed DLBCL. The regimen produced rapid disease control (ORR 100% after two cycles) and a progressive increase in CR to 80.5% by the end of treatment, indicating meaningful response deepening during the sequential phase. With a median follow-up of 28.7 months, the estimated 2-year PFS and OS were 76.1% and 81.4%, respectively, which compare favorably with historical outcomes of R-miniCHOP in patients > 80 years (2-year PFS ~ 47% and OS ~ 59%) [12]. Notably, no CNS relapses occurred despite more than half of patients having high-risk CNS-IPI scores at baseline. Together, these findings suggest that front-loading biologic control while reducing chemotherapy exposure may be a practical way to preserve curative intent in older adults who are typically undertreated or unable to tolerate standard regimens.

Although R-miniCHOP remains the most commonly used regimen for very old or frail patients who are unfit for full-dose R-CHOP [19], its efficacy remains limited, prompting investigation into alternative strategies. Previous attempts to strengthen efficacy by adding novel agents to concurrent immunochemotherapy have had mixed successes. Lenalidomide combined with R-CHOP failed to improve survival in randomized studies, and chemotherapy-intensive BTK-inhibitor regimens such as ZR-CHOP have mainly been tested in younger, fitter cohorts [20]. Although the PFS was not reached in the phase 3 ROBUST trial [21], the trends favored R2-CHOP over placebo/R-CHOP in patients with higher-risk disease. Similarly, ibrutinib combined with RCHOP demonstrated an ORR of 65% and a CR rate of 41% in patients with relapsed/refractory DLBCL, particularly in the non-GCB subtype. However, its broader adoption has been limited due to toxicity concerns, including atrial fibrillation, invasive fungal infections, and high-grade hematologic AEs.

The response kinetics and molecular patterns in our cohort provide a biologic explanation for the activity of this sequential regimen. ZR2 induction achieved rapid cytoreduction in all patients (ORR 100% after two cycles), though two-thirds remained in PR at that time (CR 33.3%, PR 66.7%), indicating that the chemotherapy-free phase primarily established early disease control rather than maximal remission. Subsequent introduction of reduced-dose miniCHOP was accompanied by clear response deepening: the CR rate increased to 72.7% by cycle 6 and to 80.5% at the end of treatment, reflecting substantial PR-to-CR conversion during the sequential program. Our genomic results support the potential significance of the BTK pathway in this population. Among patients with available sequencing, MCD and BN2 subtypes, both linked to dependence on BCR/NF-κB signaling, showed numerically deeper responses (end-of-treatment CR 80.0% in MCD and 66.7% in BN2; ORR 100% in both), in line with prior evidence that BTK inhibition is most effective in BCR-addicted DLBCL. The high CR rate observed in double-expressor cases, which comprised 41.7% of assessable patients, is also compatible with sensitivity of biologically aggressive BCR tumor to BTK-based combinations. Lastly, the absence of CNS relapse is clinically notable, as despite 54.2% of patients carrying high CNS-IPI scores, no CNS events occurred during follow-up. While exploratory, this finding suggests that continuous BTK-based therapy alongside early systemic control may contribute to CNS protection in a group otherwise predisposed to CNS failure.

From a safety standpoint, the regimen was manageable and appropriate for a high-risk elderly population. There were no treatment-related deaths, and grade 3–4 toxicities were largely hematologic and occurred predominantly after chemotherapy was introduced, which is expected in this setting. Importantly, cardiac toxicity was minimal: only one patient developed atrial fibrillation, supporting the use of zanubrutinib in older individuals with cardiovascular comorbidity, where first-generation BTK inhibitors are often problematic. Invasive fungal infections, an adverse-event signal described with some ibrutinib-based regimens, were not observed. The ability of most patients to proceed through the planned sequential program further supports tolerability, consistent with the rationale that chemotherapy-free induction may reduce early attrition in frail patients.

Clinically, these results suggest that ZR2-miniCHOP may be promising for older adults in whom full-dose R-CHOP could be used due to advanced stage, non-GCB phenotype, double-expressor biology, or high CNS-IPI risk. The regimen provides a practical way to achieve disease control while minimizing early chemotherapy burden, which is often the inflection point for treatment failure in frail patients. Moreover, our findings reinforce a treatment principle for elderly DLBCL: preserving cure depends not only on drug potency but also on sequencing and deliverability, and biologic induction before reduced-intensity chemotherapy may shift the balance toward both efficacy and feasibility.

While the incorporation of novel targeted agents (zanubrutinib and lenalidomide) inevitably increases direct medication costs compared to standard chemotherapy, this financial burden is partially offset by the regimen’s overall cost-effectiveness. The high complete response rate (80.5%) potentially circumvents the exorbitant costs associated with relapsed/refractory disease management. Furthermore, the favorable safety profile—characterized by a low incidence of severe febrile neutropenia (Grade ≥ 3: 8.7%)—prevented costly hospital readmissions and ICU utilization. Importantly, after the initial cycle, treatment was successfully transitioned to an outpatient setting, significantly reducing bed utilization and nursing care costs.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the single-arm design and modest sample size prevent definitive comparisons with R-miniCHOP, and selection bias cannot be ruled out. Furthermore, as an investigator-initiated trial where patients bore the cost of novel agents, the self-pay model inevitably introduced a selection bias, favoring patients with higher socioeconomic status and better family support. Second, patient fitness was primarily assessed using age, ECOG status, and clinical judgment. The absence of comprehensive standardized geriatric scoring systems, such as the Cumulative Illness Rating Scale-Geriatric (CIRS-G), introduces a degree of subjectivity to our frailty definition. Third, FISH testing for double- and triple-hit lymphoma was not routinely performed, limiting interpretation within biologically high-risk subsets. Fourth, as a single-center study, institutional treatment patterns and supportive-care practices may restrict generalizability. Fifth, despite follow-up exceeding two years, late relapses remain possible, and ongoing surveillance is warranted. Sixth, molecular profiling was available only for a subset, incorporated both tissue and plasma samples, and resulted in a sizeable unclassified LymphGen group, reducing power for subtype-specific analyses. This highlights the challenge of ‘financial toxicity’ in deploying novel regimens and suggests that our results may not be fully generalizable to economically disadvantaged populations without insurance coverage. Lastly, enrollment during the COVID-19 era may have affected outcomes through infection-related mortality and care disruptions, although COVID-associated deaths were reviewed and judged to be unrelated to study therapy.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In elderly or frail patients with newly diagnosed DLBCL, sequential ZR2 induction followed by response-adapted ZR2-miniCHOP achieved rapid, deep, and durable responses, with an end-of-treatment CR rate of 80.5% and 2-year PFS/OS of 76.1%/81.4% at 28.7 months’ median follow-up. No CNS relapses occurred despite high baseline CNS-IPI risk, and the regimen was generally tolerable with no treatment-related deaths and minimal cardiac toxicity. These findings suggest a clinically meaningful improvement over historical R-miniCHOP outcomes and support further validation in multicenter randomized trials incorporating geriatric assessment and patient-reported outcomes.
